title: AI Won’t Replace Your Chief of Staff. It Will Make Them More Effective.
gist: BCG's 2026 survey of 65 chiefs of staff finds AI (used by 97% of them) is reshaping rather than replacing the role: it already cuts time on board prep and decision synthesis (60-66%), is expected to absorb CEO briefing and initiative tracking within 2-3 years (~70%+), but barely touches relational work like motivating the organization (10-20%). The value of the role lies in extending CEO impact through execution, and its effectiveness hinges on CEO-controlled levers — a clear mandate (50% vs 29% highly successful), information access, decision rights and visibly signaled authority.

themes.theme: CoS value = extending CEO impact, not time

insights.claim: In BCG's 2026 survey of 65 chiefs of staff at large companies, select unicorns and nonprofits, respondents ranked driving execution of strategic priorities, clarifying and amplifying strategy, and improving decision quality as the three areas where they create the most value, each placed in the top three by at least two-thirds of respondents.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: Frames the chief of staff as an execution and decision-quality lever on the CEO agenda — relevant when assessing management bandwidth and strategy delivery capacity.
insights.locator: Where Chiefs of Staff Create the Most Value

insights.claim: Protecting and optimizing CEO time — often assumed to define the chief-of-staff role — ranked in the top three value areas for fewer than one in ten chiefs of staff surveyed by BCG.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: Challenges the 'gatekeeper' view of the role; a CoS used mainly for calendar management signals under-utilized leadership capacity.
insights.quote: the CoS creates value less by managing the CEO’s time and attention than by extending the CEO’s impact across the organization
insights.locator: At least two-thirds of respondents ranked

insights.claim: More than 70% of surveyed chiefs of staff named execution and delivery as a primary focus, followed by internal integration (60%) and decision/information management and strategy/advisory (57% each).
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: Shows the role is primarily a cross-functional execution engine, distinct from a senior executive assistant who manages schedules and logistics.
insights.locator: The distinction is important. The CoS

insights.claim: The chief of staff typically has no functional agenda of its own, allowing it to act as a neutral broker across the leadership team and the company's functions.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: Neutral-broker positioning is what lets the CoS secure cross-functional cooperation; organizations that load the role with a functional P&L may lose this.
insights.quote: “Switzerland,” as one chief of staff described it
insights.locator: Whatever the precise division of responsibilities

insights.claim: Where a company has a chief strategy officer, only 42% of chiefs of staff say strategy and advice are a primary focus, versus 71% in companies without a CSO.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: The CoS scope is a function of the rest of the C-suite — redundancy with a CSO is a design question CEOs should resolve explicitly.
insights.locator: The shape of the CoS role bends

insights.claim: When a COO is present, 67% of chiefs of staff identify execution and delivery as a primary focus versus 86% without a COO, and chiefs of staff alongside a COO tend to focus on one- to five-year horizons rather than quarterly or annual execution.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: A COO pulls the CoS toward longer-horizon strategic work; absence of a COO makes the CoS the de facto execution owner.

themes.theme: Staged AI impact on CoS work

insights.claim: 97% of chiefs of staff surveyed by BCG already use AI on the job, yet AI is reshaping rather than replacing the chief-of-staff role.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: Near-universal AI adoption at the CEO-office level is a signal of enterprise AI penetration into senior knowledge work, without headcount elimination.
insights.quote: 97% of the chiefs of staff BCG recently surveyed already use AI on the job
insights.locator: While AI is increasingly taking on parts

insights.claim: AI's impact on the chief-of-staff role is unfolding in three stages: information preparation is affected substantially today, advancing the CEO agenda is likely to yield to AI over the next two to three years, and relational work depending on judgment, trust and credibility is expected to be far less affected.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: A reusable sequencing model for which senior knowledge-work tasks automate first: preparation, then coordination/tracking, with relational work last.
insights.locator: AI Is Shifting the CoS Role’s Center of Gravity

insights.claim: AI is already reducing the time chiefs of staff spend preparing board materials (60%), organizing and facilitating executive leadership team meetings (60%) and synthesizing information to frame decisions (66%), and more than 70% expect time savings in each area within two to three years.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: Board and ELT prep is a live, proven use case for enterprise AI — supportive of vendors targeting executive synthesis and document-generation workflows.

insights.claim: Only about a third of chiefs of staff say AI currently reduces time spent briefing the CEO (34%) or aligning CEO time with organizational goals (32%), but 74% and 72% respectively expect reductions within two to three years; for overseeing CEO-led initiative execution, AI time savings are expected to rise from 40% today to 70%.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: The next wave of executive AI adoption is in briefing, priority tracking and initiative oversight — a roughly doubling of reported impact expected within 2–3 years.
insights.locator: Advancing the CEO’s Agenda: the Next Wave

insights.claim: Freeing chiefs of staff from preparation work via AI lets them focus on the decisions and judgment that follow and lets teams apply decision hygiene to AI-generated insights.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: AI value at the executive level comes from redeploying freed capacity, not just speed — governance of AI-generated insight becomes a CoS responsibility.
insights.quote: allow teams to apply suitable decision hygiene to AI-generated insights

insights.claim: Only 10% of chiefs of staff say AI currently reduces time spent inspiring and motivating the organization, and just 20% expect it to within two to three years; for managing leadership team relationships the figures are 30% and 34%, and acting as the CEO's external extension shows no expected change at 29% both today and later.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: Marks the ceiling of near-term AI substitution in leadership roles: trust, motivation and external representation remain human work.
insights.locator: Relational Work: Where AI Has Less Reach

insights.claim: Confidentiality constraints limit AI's role in senior leadership work: some chiefs of staff deliberately keep AI note-takers out of executive sessions to avoid creating a written record.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: Privacy and record-keeping concerns are a real adoption barrier for meeting-capture AI in the most sensitive executive settings.
insights.quote: The most private rooms are often the ones AI is not invited into.
insights.locator: There are good reasons for AI’s limited reach

insights.claim: Chiefs of staff rate strong stakeholder relationships (80%), CEO trust (55%) and prior experience (52%) as the leading contributors to their success.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: Success drivers are relational assets AI cannot supply, reinforcing that AI efficiency should be reinvested in relationships.
insights.locator: The Shift Won’t Happen by Itself

insights.claim: Among chiefs of staff with a formal or clearly stated mandate, 50% describe themselves as highly successful versus 29% of those operating under a looser understanding, yet only about half have such a mandate and two-thirds say an unclear or shifting mandate limits their effectiveness.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: Mandate clarity is the cheapest lever for CEO-office effectiveness; ambiguity is widespread and measurably costly.
insights.quote: “The issue with the chief of staff role is that every organization has a different interpretation.”

insights.claim: 42% of chiefs of staff cite information parity as a constraint, rising to 47% among those who participate in executive leadership team decisions versus 21% of those who do not.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: The more decision-making weight a CoS carries, the more information exclusion hurts — CEOs should audit forums and distribution lists the CoS is excluded from.
insights.quote: the CoS sees what the CEO sees when the CEO sees it

insights.claim: 28% of chiefs of staff say insufficient delegation limits their effectiveness, including 37% of more junior chiefs of staff versus 20% of those at VP level or above; delegation models vary widely, with one CoS's line drawn at capital commitments approaching $5 million.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: Decision rights scale with seniority; explicit thresholds (e.g., capital limits) make delegated authority workable.

insights.claim: 26% of chiefs of staff say the CEO's failure to signal their authority to the leadership team limits their effectiveness; authority accrues when the CEO visibly and repeatedly routes work through the CoS, since teams quickly notice if a CoS can be bypassed.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: CEO behavior, not formal titles, determines whether the CoS role has real influence — a leadership-quality signal for observers of management.
insights.quote: Teams mirror what the CEO tolerates, quickly noticing if a CoS can be bypassed.

insights.claim: Organizations can either use AI to streamline the existing chief-of-staff job, producing a more efficient CoS, or redesign the role around evolving strategic priorities to produce a more consequential one — and as AI absorbs traditional duties, redesign may become a necessity rather than an opportunity.
insights.speaker: Christine Barton
insights.so_what: Generalizes to AI-exposed knowledge roles: the payoff from AI depends on deliberate redeployment of freed capacity, not automation alone.
insights.quote: The first produces a more efficient chief of staff. The second can result in a more consequential one.
